subChunks.title: Research Design, Validity & Reliability
subChunks.hookHtml:
In 2015, the Open Science Collaboration published a landmark analysis: they attempted to replicate 100 studies from top psychology journals. Only 36 to 39 of them successfully replicated — depending on the criteria used. Effect sizes were, on average, half those reported in the original studies. This was not a fringe journal or a niche topic: it was the core empirical literature of scientific psychology.

Understanding research methods in psychology is not a technical afterthought — it is the foundation upon which evidence-based claims are built or demolished. A psychologist who cannot evaluate research design cannot evaluate evidence, and cannot make defensible clinical or policy decisions.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Research Designs

Experimental designs are the gold standard for establishing causation. The researcher manipulates an independent variable (IV) and measures a dependent variable (DV) while controlling extraneous variables (EVs). Random allocation to conditions equates participant characteristics across groups, making the experimental and control groups comparable at baseline.

Three main experimental designs: independent groups (different participants in each condition) — avoids order effects but requires larger samples and is susceptible to participant variables. Repeated measures (same participants in all conditions) — controls participant variables and requires fewer participants, but risks order effects (counterbalancing mitigates these). Matched pairs — matches participants on key variables before random allocation; intermediate between the two.

Quasi-experimental designs manipulate an IV but do not use random allocation (e.g., comparing schools that did vs. did not adopt a programme). They support causal inference more strongly than correlational research but less strongly than true experiments because pre-existing group differences cannot be ruled out.

Correlational research examines the statistical relationship between two measured variables without manipulation. A correlation coefficient (r) ranges from −1 (perfect negative) to +1 (perfect positive), with 0 indicating no linear relationship. Correlation does not establish causation: directionality (which variable causes which) and third variable problems (a hidden variable explaining both) cannot be ruled out from correlational data alone.

Validity and Reliability

Internal validity is the extent to which observed changes in the DV can be attributed to the IV, rather than confounding variables. Threats include: demand characteristics (participants guessing study aims and modifying behaviour), experimenter effects (researcher expectations influencing data), and lack of experimental control.

External validity is the extent to which findings generalise beyond the specific study. Population validity: whether the sample represents the broader population. WEIRD samples (Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic; Henrich et al., 2010) have dominated psychological research, limiting generalisation to other populations. Ecological validity: whether the research context reflects real-world conditions. Laboratory experiments sacrifice ecological validity for control; observational field studies sacrifice control for ecological validity.

Reliability refers to consistency of measurement. Test-retest reliability: the same measure produces consistent results over time (r > 0.8 is typically acceptable). Inter-rater reliability: independent coders produce consistent ratings of the same data (measured by Cohen's kappa κ). Internal consistency: items within a scale measure the same underlying construct (Cronbach's alpha α ≥ 0.7).

Ethical Principles

The British Psychological Society (BPS) Code of Ethics and Conduct (2021) identifies four overarching principles: respect (autonomy, privacy, informed consent), competence, responsibility (duty of care, avoiding harm), and integrity (honesty, transparency). Informed consent must be obtained before participation, with the right to withdraw and full debriefing afterwards. Deception is permissible only when scientifically necessary, when no less deceptive alternative exists, and when participants would not have objected had they known the full aims — requiring independent ethical committee approval. Milgram's (1963) and Zimbardo's (1971) Stanford Prison Experiment are canonical ethical failures against which contemporary standards are benchmarked.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen projects the 2015 Open Science Collaboration replication figure: 36–39 out of 100 studies replicated. Several students look surprised.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: The replication crisis is not a scandal that happened to psychology from outside. It was generated from within — by publication bias, by small samples, by the practice of p-hacking: testing multiple hypotheses or outcomes and reporting only the significant ones. It is a methodological crisis, and it is solvable with methodological rigour.
She draws a two-by-two matrix: HIGH/LOW internal validity on one axis, HIGH/LOW ecological validity on the other.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Every research design is a trade-off. Laboratory experiments give you control — high internal validity. But your participants know they're in a study, your setting is artificial, and your sample is probably undergraduates at a Western university. Real-world studies give you ecological validity but you cannot rule out confounds.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Ethical principles are not obstacles to research — they are its foundation. Milgram's findings are genuinely important. But the distress his participants experienced was real, and the precedent it set had to be stopped. The BPS Code exists because previous generations of researchers got it badly wrong.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Guided Practice — Designing and Critiquing a Study

Scenario: A researcher wants to investigate whether mindfulness meditation reduces self-reported anxiety in university students. She plans to advertise for volunteers, randomly assign them to either an 8-week mindfulness course (experimental group) or a waiting list (control group), and measure anxiety using a standardised questionnaire at the start and end of the 8 weeks.

Evaluate this research design. In your answer: (1) identify two methodological strengths of the design; (2) identify two threats to internal or external validity and explain how each could affect the findings; (3) outline one change the researcher could make to improve the design; and (4) identify at least one ethical consideration specific to this study.

Guidance: Use precise research methods terminology (IV, DV, demand characteristics, WEIRD sample, etc.). Aim for 130–160 words.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Independent Practice — Evaluating the Replication Crisis

Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn (2011) demonstrated through simulation that flexible analysis practices — including testing multiple dependent variables, collecting data until significance is achieved (optional stopping), and including or excluding participants selectively — can produce a false positive rate of up to 61%, despite p < .05 appearing to guarantee only a 5% false positive rate. They coined the term 'researcher degrees of freedom' to describe these practices.

Evaluate the implications of researcher degrees of freedom and the broader replication crisis for the credibility of psychological research. In your answer, explain what p-hacking is and why it inflates false positive rates, consider what structural features of science (publication bias, career incentives) encourage these practices, and evaluate the methodological reforms proposed to address them (pre-registration, open data, open materials, larger samples, replication studies). Reach a conclusion about whether the replication crisis has strengthened or weakened the scientific credibility of psychology overall.

Write at least 160 words in paragraphs. This is an evaluative essay — do not list reforms without assessing them.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Researcher degrees of freedom — the flexibility researchers have in collecting, analysing, and reporting data — generate false positives through a family-wise error rate problem. When a researcher tests multiple dependent variables, applies multiple exclusion criteria, or continues data collection until p < .05 is reached, the probability of finding at least one significant result by chance vastly exceeds the nominal alpha level. Simmons et al.'s (2011) demonstration that these practices alone can produce 61% false positive rates exposes a fundamental flaw not in individual researchers' ethics, but in the incentive structure of scientific publication: journals reward novel significant findings, not null results or careful replications.

Structural factors amplify the problem. Publication bias — the tendency for significant results to be published and null results to remain in file drawers — means that the published literature systematically overstates effect sizes and underestimates replication failure rates. Career incentives reward high-impact publications, not methodological caution, creating rational pressure to pursue significance by any available means.

The reform agenda is substantive. Pre-registration — committing to hypotheses, design, and analysis plan before data collection — eliminates most researcher degrees of freedom post hoc. It is now supported by major journals (via Registered Reports), the Open Science Framework, and the APA. Open data and open materials mandates enable independent verification and replication at minimal marginal cost. Requirements for larger samples with adequate statistical power (many classic studies were powered to detect implausibly large effects) reduce false positive rates and improve precision.

The replication crisis has, paradoxically, strengthened psychology's long-term scientific credibility by forcing the field to confront methodological problems that other sciences also have but have not yet systematically addressed. The reforms implemented since 2011 — while imperfectly adopted — represent genuine progress toward a more robust science. Psychology is not uniquely flawed; it is uniquely self-critical. The field that ran 270 replication attempts (Open Science Collaboration, 2015) is showing greater scientific maturity than one that never tried.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a school student why a correlation between two variables does not prove that one causes the other. Give two concrete examples — one showing a directionality problem, one showing a third-variable problem.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The extent to which a study's results can be attributed to the independent variable rather than confounding variables. The fundamental criterion for causal inference.
The extent to which a study's findings reflect real-world conditions. High laboratory control typically sacrifices ecological validity; field studies sacrifice control.

Henrich et al.'s (2010) acronym for the dominant participant pool in psychology research: Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic — limiting the generalisability of most published findings.

Flexible data analysis practices (testing multiple outcomes, optional stopping, selective participant exclusion) that inflate the false positive rate while maintaining the appearance of a p < .05 significance threshold.
The practice of publicly committing to hypotheses, study design, and analysis plan before data collection begins, to prevent post hoc flexibility from inflating false positive rates.
The degree of agreement between independent raters or coders of the same data. Measured by Cohen's kappa (κ); essential for observational and interview-based research validity.

questions.questionHtml: Which research design provides the strongest basis for establishing causal relationships between variables?
options: True experimental design with random allocation
Quasi-experimental design with matched groups
Correlational design with large samples
Cross-sectional observational design
questions.correctAnswer: True experimental design with random allocation

questions.questionHtml: True or False: A correlation coefficient of r = −0.75 indicates a stronger relationship between two variables than a correlation of r = +0.60.

A researcher studying prejudice in school children uses a standardised questionnaire. She tests the same children three months later with the same questionnaire and finds very similar scores. She then has two colleagues independently code children's playground observations and finds their codings are highly consistent. Which two forms of reliability has she demonstrated?
options: Test-retest reliability and inter-rater reliability
Internal consistency and ecological validity
Construct validity and population validity
Test-retest reliability and internal consistency

questions.questionHtml: Henrich et al.'s (2010) 'WEIRD' critique of psychological research primarily challenges which type of validity?
options: Population validity (and therefore external validity)
Internal validity
Ecological validity
Construct validity

subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
The study has one clear strength: random assignment to conditions equates participant characteristics at baseline, supporting internal validity and permitting causal inference about the effect of mindfulness on anxiety (Campbell & Stanley, 1963).

Two significant limitations undermine confidence. First, advertising for volunteers introduces self-selection bias: participants who choose to enrol in a mindfulness study may already be motivated to reduce anxiety, or may hold positive expectations that inflate self-reported improvement independently of the intervention (demand characteristics). This threatens both internal and population validity.

Second, a waiting-list control does not adequately control for non-specific effects — social contact, therapist attention, and positive expectations may account for improvement rather than mindfulness per se. An active control condition (e.g., structured relaxation training) matched for time and attention would isolate the specific ingredient of mindfulness, substantially strengthening causal inference.

subChunks.title: Quantitative & Qualitative Analysis
subChunks.hookHtml:
Numbers and narratives: psychology uses both, and the tension between them is productive. Quantitative methods allow measurement of behaviour at scale, statistical inference about populations, and the testing of hypotheses against the baseline of chance. Qualitative methods explore meaning, experience, and the texture of human lives in ways that numbers cannot capture — but at the cost of statistical generalisability.

Understanding when each approach is appropriate, what each can and cannot establish, and how to evaluate the quality of each is essential for a psychologist who reads and generates research.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Quantitative Analysis

Descriptive statistics summarise data. Measures of central tendency: the mean (arithmetic average; sensitive to outliers), median (middle value; robust to outliers), and mode (most frequent value). Measures of spread: the standard deviation (average deviation from the mean; the most commonly reported measure of variability in psychological research).

Inferential statistics allow conclusions about populations from samples. The logic of null hypothesis significance testing (NHST): assume the null hypothesis (H₀; no effect) is true, calculate the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed by chance (the p-value), and reject H₀ if p < .05 (convention). A p-value is not the probability that H₀ is true; it is the probability of the observed data given H₀. This distinction is frequently confused.

Effect size measures the magnitude of an effect independent of sample size. Cohen's d (standardised mean difference) and Pearson's r are the most common. By convention (Cohen, 1988): d = 0.2 (small), 0.5 (medium), 0.8 (large). A statistically significant result with a very large sample may have a negligible effect size; a large effect may fail to reach significance in a very small sample. Effect size and confidence intervals (CIs) should always be reported alongside p-values.

Meta-analysis statistically combines results from multiple studies on the same question, producing a pooled effect size estimate with greater precision than any single study. The quality of a meta-analysis depends on the quality and representativeness of included studies (publication bias inflates meta-analytic effect sizes). Funnel plots can reveal asymmetry suggesting publication bias.

Qualitative Research

Qualitative methods generate rich, in-depth data about subjective experience, meaning-making, and social processes. They are particularly appropriate for: exploring novel phenomena with no established theory; understanding lived experience of mental health conditions; investigating how individuals construct meaning from events.

Thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006) is the most widely used qualitative method in psychology. Researchers read and re-read data (transcripts, interview responses) to identify patterns of meaning — codes — which are organised into broader themes. Reflexive thematic analysis emphasises the researcher's active role in theme construction rather than 'finding' pre-existing themes in data. Quality is assessed by credibility (are themes grounded in data?), transferability (can findings be applied to similar contexts?), and reflexivity (has the researcher acknowledged their own influence on interpretation?).

Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) (Smith, Flowers & Larkin, 2009) focuses on how individuals make sense of significant personal experiences. It uses small, purposively selected samples (typically 4–10 participants); breadth is sacrificed for depth. Quality criteria include sensitivity to context, commitment to participants' perspective, and a coherent hermeneutic approach.

Mixed Methods

Mixed methods research combines quantitative and qualitative approaches, typically to achieve complementarity (each approach addressing what the other cannot). A randomised controlled trial of a new psychological therapy might be complemented by qualitative interviews exploring participants' experiences of the therapy — the quantitative component tells you whether it works; the qualitative component tells you why and for whom. Creswell & Plano Clark (2017) provide the standard framework for mixed methods design.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen projects two excerpts side by side: a table of means and standard deviations from a depression RCT; and three lines from an IPA study — a participant describing the moment they realised they were getting better. 'Which one tells you more about depression?' she asks.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: The RCT tells you the average effect for a sample of two hundred people. It cannot tell you whether this particular person's experience was captured by that average, or whether the change they experienced felt meaningful to them. Both questions matter. They need different tools.
She writes p < .05 on the board. Underlines it. Then writes: 'Prob(data | H₀)'. Not 'Prob(H₀ | data)'.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: This is the most common misunderstanding in all of quantitative psychology. The p-value is the probability of your data if the null hypothesis were true — not the probability that the null is false. Researchers, reviewers, and textbooks get this wrong constantly. Don't be one of them.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Effect size is what actually matters for clinical and practical decision-making. A new therapy that significantly outperforms placebo in an n of 5,000 with d = 0.08 is statistically significant and clinically meaningless. A d of 0.8 in a small study — if it replicates — is clinically important. Learn to read effect sizes.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Guided Practice — Interpreting Research Findings

Scenario: A researcher reports the following: 'A new mindfulness app significantly reduced anxiety in a sample of 847 university students compared to a waitlist control group (p = .03, d = 0.11, 95% CI [0.04, 0.18]).'

Critically evaluate what this finding tells us and what it does not. In your answer: explain what p = .03 means and what it does not mean; evaluate the clinical significance of d = 0.11 using Cohen's (1988) conventions; explain the role of the large sample size in producing statistical significance; and comment on at least one external validity concern. Use precise statistical terminology throughout.

Guidance: The effect size interpretation is the key analytical skill here. Aim for 120–150 words. Do not simply describe what each statistic is — evaluate what they tell us about the study's importance.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Independent Practice — Qualitative vs. Quantitative Research

A clinical psychology research team wants to investigate the experience of post-traumatic growth (positive psychological change following trauma) in cancer survivors. A senior researcher argues that a quantitative survey measuring post-traumatic growth on a standardised scale (administered to n = 300) is preferable because it allows statistical comparison across demographic groups and produces generalisable findings. A junior researcher argues that an IPA study with n = 8 participants would provide richer, more meaningful insights into how survivors make sense of their experience.

Evaluate both positions. In your answer, identify the specific questions each design can and cannot answer, consider how their quality criteria differ (reliability and validity for quantitative; credibility, transferability, and reflexivity for qualitative), and propose a mixed methods design that would address the limitations of each approach individually. Justify your design decisions with reference to methodological principles.

Write at least 160 words in paragraphs.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The quantitative survey and the IPA study address fundamentally different research questions, and evaluating them against each other as though they are competing approaches to the same question misunderstands the logic of each methodology.

A standardised post-traumatic growth scale administered to n = 300 can determine whether growth occurs at detectable rates in this population, whether it varies by gender, age, cancer type, or time since diagnosis, and how it correlates with other measured variables. This produces statistically generalisable findings about group-level patterns. However, such a scale — necessarily constructed from predefined items — cannot capture whether survivors experience growth in ways that the scale's designers anticipated, nor the meaning-making processes through which growth occurs. High scores on a standardised scale and genuine psychological transformation may not be the same thing.

An IPA study with n = 8 can explore in granular detail how individual survivors understand and narrate their experience of change — what growth felt like, how it conflicted with grief, which relationships were central to it. Quality is judged by credibility (are themes richly grounded in participants' accounts?), transferability (can findings inform understanding of similar populations?), and the researcher's reflexivity (how do their own values shape their interpretations?). The findings cannot be generalised statistically to a population of 300, but they generate theory and hypotheses that quantitative research can then test.

A mixed methods design is well-suited to this topic. A sequential explanatory design (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2017) would first administer the quantitative survey to n = 300 to establish group-level patterns, then purposively select 8–10 participants representing diverse survey response profiles for IPA interviews. The quantitative component identifies where growth is occurring (and where it is not); the qualitative component explains the mechanisms and meanings that the numbers cannot access. This achieves complementarity: each approach addresses what the other cannot, producing a more complete picture of post-traumatic growth than either methodology alone.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a school student the difference between a p-value and an effect size. Why might a study show p < .05 but still not be clinically meaningful? Use a simple concrete example.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A standardised measure of the magnitude of an effect, independent of sample size. Cohen's d and Pearson's r are most common; d = 0.2/0.5/0.8 = small/medium/large by convention (Cohen, 1988).
The probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Commonly misinterpreted as the probability that the null hypothesis is false.
A statistical technique for combining results from multiple independent studies on the same question to produce a pooled, more precise estimate of the effect size.

Braun & Clarke's (2006) qualitative method for identifying, analysing, and reporting patterns of meaning (themes) within data. Now widely used in reflexive form, emphasising researcher agency in theme construction.
Smith, Flowers & Larkin's (2009) qualitative approach examining how individuals make sense of significant personal experiences. Uses small, purposive samples; prioritises depth over breadth.

A range of values within which the true population parameter is estimated to lie with a specified probability (typically 95%). Narrow CIs indicate more precise estimates; they should always accompany p-values.

questions.questionHtml: Using Cohen's (1988) conventions, a standardised mean difference of d = 0.5 represents which effect size?
options: Medium effect size
Small effect size
Large effect size
Negligible effect size

questions.questionHtml: True or False: A p-value of .03 means there is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true given the observed data.

A researcher conducts a qualitative study on the experience of anxiety in adolescents, interviewing 7 participants in depth. She shares her emerging themes with participants to check whether they feel the themes accurately reflect their experience. This process is called:
options: Member checking (respondent validation)
Counterbalancing
Stratified sampling
Matched pairs design

questions.questionHtml: A pharmaceutical company reports that their new antidepressant is significantly more effective than placebo (p = .001, d = 0.15, N = 3,000). The most important critical evaluation of this claim is:
options: The effect size is trivially small despite statistical significance, suggesting limited clinical relevance
The p-value is too small to be credible in a study this size
A qualitative study should have been used instead to assess patient experience
The study should have used a repeated measures rather than independent groups design
questions.correctAnswer: The effect size is trivially small despite statistical significance, suggesting limited clinical relevance

subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Although p = .03 indicates statistical significance — the probability of obtaining this result by chance, given a true null effect, is 3% — it does not indicate practical or clinical importance. With N = 847, statistical power is very high, meaning even negligible true effects will reliably produce significant p-values.

The critical statistic is the effect size. Cohen's (1988) conventions classify d = 0.11 as negligible — well below the threshold for a small effect (d = 0.20). The 95% confidence interval [0.04, 0.18] excludes zero, but all plausible true effects remain clinically trivial. The app reduces anxiety by less than a tenth of a standard deviation.

This finding exemplifies the distinction between statistical and practical significance: the mindfulness app 'works' in a narrow statistical sense but produces no meaningful reduction in anxiety. Clinicians and commissioners must prioritise effect sizes alongside p-values when evaluating whether an intervention warrants adoption at scale.

subChunks.title: Descriptive Statistics in R — A First Practical
subChunks.hookHtml:
Statistics is not a separate skill from psychology — it is psychology, as expressed in numbers. If you cannot read a result, you cannot evaluate the claim that comes with it. If you cannot compute a result, you cannot test your own hypothesis.

R is the dominant statistical language in academic psychology and clinical research. It is free, reproducible, and used in every Russell Group psychology department. This sub-chunk is your first hands-on encounter with R — running code directly in your browser via WebR (R compiled to WebAssembly). You will compute the most fundamental statistical summaries: means, medians, standard deviations.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Why R, Not SPSS?

SPSS dominated psychology for decades. R has overtaken it for three reasons: it is free (SPSS licences cost institutions thousands per year); it is reproducible (your analysis is a script, not a sequence of clicks); and it has a thriving open-source ecosystem (over 18,000 packages on CRAN as of 2023). Every major psychology journal now accepts R analyses, and many require code-sharing as a condition of publication.

Descriptive Statistics — The Foundation

Before any inferential test, you describe your data. Descriptive statistics fall into three families:

Measures of central tendency:

  • Mean — the arithmetic average. In R: mean(x). Sensitive to outliers — one extreme score pulls the mean toward it.
  • Median — the middle value when data are ordered. In R: median(x). Robust to outliers; the standard choice for skewed distributions (e.g., reaction times, income).
  • Mode — the most frequent value. R has no built-in mode() for statistics (that function returns data type). Use names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1].

Measures of spread:

  • Range — max minus min. In R: max(x) - min(x) or diff(range(x)).
  • Variance — average squared deviation from the mean. In R: var(x). Uses n−1 (Bessel's correction) by default, treating data as a sample.
  • Standard deviation (SD) — square root of variance, in original units. In R: sd(x). The most reported spread measure in psychology.
  • Interquartile range (IQR) — Q3 − Q1. In R: IQR(x). Robust to outliers, used alongside the median.

Measures of shape:

  • Skewness — asymmetry. Positive skew: tail on the right (e.g., income). Negative skew: tail on the left (e.g., exam scores in a hard test).
  • Kurtosis — tail heaviness. High kurtosis = heavy tails (more outliers than a normal distribution).

Working with Data in R

In R, data are stored in vectors (1-D) or data frames (2-D, like a spreadsheet). The c() function combines values into a vector:

scores <- c(72, 85, 91, 68, 77, 83, 88, 75, 79, 81)

The <- operator is R's assignment. scores now holds 10 numbers. Apply summary statistics directly:

mean(scores)    # 79.9
median(scores)  # 80.0
sd(scores)      # 7.262

For psychological research, you will almost always work with data frames loaded from a CSV file. R's summary() function gives a one-line overview of any vector or data frame column:

summary(scores)
#  Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
#  68.0   75.5    80.0    79.9   84.5    91.0

Interpreting the Output

A descriptive summary is not the end of analysis — it is the beginning. Always ask: does the mean match the median? (If not, the distribution is skewed.) Is the SD large or small relative to the mean? (Coefficient of variation = SD/mean; values above 0.3 suggest substantial variability.) Are there outliers, and how were they identified? (A common rule: values more than 1.5 × IQR beyond Q1 or Q3.)

What's Next

This sub-chunk is the first of a sequence that will take you from these basics through t-tests, ANOVA, regression, and multivariate methods, all in R. By the end of the Foundation tier, you will be able to run a complete one-way ANOVA with effect sizes and write up the results in APA format. By the end of the Capstone Empirical Project, you will be analysing a real anonymised psychology dataset and producing a publication-ready report.

Independent Practice — A Full Descriptive Summary

A new dataset is loaded: iq, a vector of IQ scores from a sample of 20 university students. Without any scaffolding, write R code that:

  1. Computes the mean and assigns it to iq_mean
  2. Computes the median and assigns it to iq_median

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to someone who has never used R what the difference is between the mean and the median, and why a psychologist studying reaction times might choose to report the median instead of the mean.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A one-dimensional ordered collection of values of the same type. Created with c(); the fundamental data structure in R.
The use of n−1 (rather than n) in the variance/SD formula to give an unbiased estimate of population variance from a sample. R's var() and sd() use n−1 by default.
SD divided by the mean. A standardised measure of dispersion useful for comparing variability across datasets with different units or scales.
The Comprehensive R Archive Network — the official repository of R packages. Over 18,000 packages as of 2023, including all major psychology analysis tools.
A measure of distribution asymmetry. Positive skew = right tail (mean > median); negative skew = left tail (mean < median); zero = symmetric.
R compiled to WebAssembly, allowing R code to run directly in a web browser without server-side R installation. Used by Arcane Academy to teach statistics interactively.

var()

A researcher reports the following reaction-time data: mean = 580 ms, median = 510 ms. What does this tell you about the distribution?
options: Positively skewed — a few slow responses are pulling the mean above the median

subChunks.title: Comparing Groups in R — t-Tests
subChunks.hookHtml: The t-test is the workhorse of psychological research. Whether you're asking "did this therapy reduce anxiety?" or "do women and men score differently on this measure?" you need a method that compares two groups while accounting for natural variability in the data — because random fluctuation alone can produce apparent differences. The t-test quantifies exactly this: the ratio of the observed difference to what you'd expect from chance alone. A large t-statistic means the observed difference is unlikely to be noise. R makes it a single function call. Understanding what that function is doing — and when to use which variant — is what separates a psychologist who can run statistics from one who can interpret them.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Logic of the t-Test

All t-tests share the same underlying logic: they divide a signal (the difference you observed) by noise (the variability you'd expect from sampling error). The general form is:

t = observed difference / standard error of the difference

A t-statistic of 1 means the observed difference is the same size as typical chance variation. A t of 5 means the difference is five times larger than what chance produces — very unlikely to arise from sampling error alone. The t-statistic is then referred to a t-distribution with a specific number of degrees of freedom (df) to obtain a p-value: the probability of observing a t at least this large if the null hypothesis (no true difference) is correct. Three variants of the t-test address three different research designs.

One-Sample t-Test

Tests whether a sample mean differs significantly from a hypothesised population value (the null hypothesis). For example: is the mean IQ of psychology students different from the population mean of 100?

scores <- c(108, 112, 99, 115, 103, 107, 111, 98, 114, 106)
t.test(scores, mu = 100)   # mu = hypothesised population mean

In R, t.test() returns a list with: $statistic (the t-value), $parameter (df), $p.value, $conf.int (95% CI for the mean), and $estimate (the sample mean).

Independent Samples t-Test

Tests whether two unrelated groups differ on a continuous measure. For example: do CBT and waitlist control participants have different anxiety scores at follow-up?

# Vector syntax:
t.test(cbt_scores, control_scores)

# Formula syntax (requires a data frame with columns 'score' and 'group'):
t.test(score ~ group, data = df)

R uses Welch's t-test by default (var.equal = FALSE). Welch's test adjusts the degrees of freedom to account for unequal variances between groups — it is more conservative than Student's t-test but is the appropriate default because assuming equal variances is rarely justified. The Welch df is often fractional (e.g., df = 27.3), produced by the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation. To use Student's t-test (equal variances assumed): t.test(x, y, var.equal = TRUE).

Paired t-Test

Tests whether scores differ between two related measurements — before and after an intervention on the same participants, or matched-pairs designs. The paired t-test converts the two sets of scores into a single vector of differences and runs a one-sample t-test on those differences against zero.

t.test(pre, post, paired = TRUE)

Using paired = TRUE is essential — failing to do so on paired data runs an independent samples test, which ignores the correlation between pre and post scores and produces inflated standard errors (reduced power). The degrees of freedom for a paired t-test are n − 1 (where n is the number of pairs).

Effect Size: Cohen's d

The p-value tells you whether the effect is distinguishable from chance; it does not tell you how large the effect is. Cohen's d expresses the difference in standard deviation units. By convention (Cohen, 1988): d = 0.2 (small), 0.5 (medium), 0.8 (large). A clinically meaningful treatment effect for anxiety typically requires d ≥ 0.5; anything below 0.2 is negligible regardless of p-value.

Paired data:

d <- mean(pre - post) / sd(pre - post)

Independent groups:

pooled_sd <- sqrt(
  (var(x) * (length(x) - 1) + var(y) * (length(y) - 1)) /
  (length(x) + length(y) - 2)
)
d <- (mean(x) - mean(y)) / pooled_sd

Note: d is directional — a negative d means the first group scored lower. Always report the absolute value with a direction statement in the text, or frame the subtraction to produce a positive value (pre − post for an expected improvement).

Checking Assumptions

Both t-tests assume the data are approximately normally distributed (or that n is large enough for the Central Limit Theorem to ensure normality of the sampling distribution). The Shapiro-Wilk test tests normality formally — but with small samples (n < 50) it has low power, and with large samples it flags trivial departures. Use it as a guide alongside visual inspection:

shapiro.test(x)          # p > .05 consistent with normality
qqnorm(x); qqline(x)    # Q-Q plot: points on line = normal

For independent samples: if groups have markedly different standard deviations (ratio > 2:1), prefer Welch's test (the default). The paired t-test only requires normality of the differences, not of the raw scores separately.

APA Reporting Format

Standard APA 7 format for a paired t-test result:

A paired-samples t-test indicated that anxiety scores were significantly lower after CBT (M = 29.87, SD = 5.35) than before (M = 41.00, SD = 7.23), t(14) = 13.56, p < .001, d = 3.50.

Key elements: degrees of freedom in parentheses, two-tailed p-value (unless one-tailed is explicitly justified a priori), Cohen's d effect size. The p-value is reported to three decimal places; if it is below .001, write p < .001 rather than p = .000.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen's laptop is connected to the projector. She opens a dataset of anxiety scores from a CBT pilot study — 15 clients assessed before and after an 8-week intervention.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: We could just subtract the means and eyeball it. The average dropped from 41 to 30 — obviously better. But 'obviously better' is not publishable. We need to know: is a drop of this size, in a sample of 15, distinguishable from chance? That is exactly the question a t-test answers.
She types: result <- t.test(pre, post, paired = TRUE). The output appears: t(14) = 13.56, p < 2.2e-16.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: p < 2.2e-16. That is R's way of saying the probability is vanishingly small. Now compute the effect size. d = mean(pre - post) / sd(pre - post). In this dataset that gives d ≈ 3.5. By Cohen's conventions that is enormous — but remember, this is a small pilot study with a non-randomised design. Large effects in small convenience samples rarely survive replication at full scale.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: One question I hear constantly: when do I use paired versus independent? The answer is always in the design. If the same people are measured twice — before and after, or matched pairs — use paired. If the two groups are entirely different people, use independent. Using the wrong one is not a minor technical error; it changes the answer you get.

She shows side by side: t.test(pre, post) and t.test(pre, post, paired = TRUE). The t-statistics differ substantially. The paired test is more sensitive because it removes between-person variability from the error term.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Report it in APA format. Not 'p was very small.' Not 't was large.' Exactly this: t(14) = 13.56, p < .001, d = 3.50. The number in parentheses is the degrees of freedom. Everything that follows is reproducible from your code — which means anyone can check it.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a fellow student who missed today's lecture the difference between a paired and an independent samples t-test. Give one example of a psychology study that would correctly use each. What goes wrong if you use the independent version on paired data?

rabbitHoleTerms.definition: The default t-test in R, which adjusts degrees of freedom using the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation to handle unequal variances between groups. More conservative than Student's t-test but the appropriate default because assuming equal variances is rarely warranted.

The number of independent pieces of information in the data available to estimate a parameter. For a paired t-test: n − 1. For independent samples: approximately n₁ + n₂ − 2 (Welch adjusts this downward). Larger df → t-distribution approaches the normal distribution.

A standardised effect size measure expressing the difference between groups in standard deviation units. Conventions (Cohen, 1988): 0.2 = small, 0.5 = medium, 0.8 = large. Computed differently for paired vs independent designs.

A formal test of normality in R: shapiro.test(x). p > .05 is consistent with normality. Low power with small samples and high power with large samples, so always inspect Q-Q plots alongside the formal test.

rabbitHoleTerms.term: Type I and Type II Error
rabbitHoleTerms.definition: Type I error (false positive): rejecting H₀ when it is true; rate = alpha (conventionally .05). Type II error (false negative): failing to reject H₀ when it is false; rate = beta. Power = 1 − beta. These trade off: reducing alpha increases Type II error rate.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher measures depression scores in the same 20 participants before and after a mindfulness intervention. Which t-test variant is correct, and what are the degrees of freedom?
options: Paired t-test; df = 19
Independent samples t-test; df = 38
Paired t-test; df = 20
Independent samples t-test; df = 19
questions.explanationHtml: Because the same participants provide both measurements, a paired t-test is correct — it removes between-person variability from the error term. The degrees of freedom for a paired t-test are n − 1 = 20 − 1 = 19, where n is the number of pairs (participants), not the total number of observations.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher compares working memory scores between two independent groups: adults with ADHD (n = 30) and neurotypical adults (n = 30). She runs t.test(adhd, control) in R and obtains: t(52.4) = 3.21, p = .002, 95% CI [2.1, 8.9]. What does the fractional degrees of freedom (52.4) indicate?
options: A data entry error — degrees of freedom must be a whole number
R applied Welch's correction for potentially unequal group variances, which produces a non-integer df via the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation
The result is based on a one-tailed test, which adjusts the degrees of freedom
The sample sizes are unequal after listwise deletion of missing data
questions.correctAnswer: R applied Welch's correction for potentially unequal group variances, which produces a non-integer df via the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation
questions.explanationHtml: R's default t.test() uses Welch's t-test (var.equal = FALSE), which adjusts the degrees of freedom using the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation to account for potentially unequal variances between groups. This produces a fractional df that is typically lower than the Student's t-test df (n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 58). This is the statistically appropriate default and is not an error.

questions.questionHtml: A paired t-test produces t(24) = 2.15, p = .042, d = 0.44. Which is the most complete and accurate interpretation for a journal write-up?
options: The intervention significantly reduced anxiety scores (p < .05)
The intervention produced a statistically significant but modest reduction in anxiety scores, t(24) = 2.15, p = .042, d = 0.44
The intervention significantly improved outcomes, confirming the hypothesis
There was a significant difference between conditions, but the effect was too small to be clinically meaningful
questions.correctAnswer: The intervention produced a statistically significant but modest reduction in anxiety scores, t(24) = 2.15, p = .042, d = 0.44
questions.explanationHtml: APA format requires reporting the full test statistic including df, exact p-value, and effect size. d = 0.44 is between small (0.2) and medium (0.5) by Cohen's conventions — clinically modest. A complete write-up states the statistical result with all required numbers and contextualises the effect size. Reporting only p < .05 is insufficient; characterising the effect as 'too small to be clinically meaningful' without reference to the specific context oversteps what the statistics alone can establish.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: In R, running t.test(pre, post) on paired data produces the same result as t.test(pre, post, paired = TRUE).
questions.explanationHtml: Without paired = TRUE, R treats pre and post as two independent groups and runs a Welch independent-samples t-test. This ignores the correlation between pre and post scores, uses a different error term (larger, because it does not remove between-person variability), and produces a different — and incorrect — t-statistic and p-value. The paired test is substantially more powerful for repeated-measures designs because it eliminates individual differences from the denominator.

subChunks.title: Correlation & Simple Regression in R
subChunks.hookHtml: Does social support predict stress? Does sleep quality relate to academic performance? These questions ask not whether two groups differ, but whether two continuous variables move together — and if so, whether we can use one to predict the other. Correlation quantifies the strength and direction of a linear relationship. Regression goes further: it gives you an equation to predict one variable from another, and it partitions how much of the variation in the outcome the predictor explains. Together, these are the most widely used analytical tools in health, clinical, and social psychology. In R, both are a few lines of code. The interpretive challenge — understanding what the numbers mean and what they cannot tell you — is where the real skill lies.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Correlation: Pearson's r and Spearman's rho

Pearson's r measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables. It ranges from −1 (perfect negative linear relationship) to +1 (perfect positive), with 0 indicating no linear relationship. Squaring r gives the coefficient of determination (r²): the proportion of variance in one variable explained by the linear relationship with the other.

cor_result <- cor.test(x, y)   # Pearson's r with hypothesis test
cor_result$estimate             # the r value
cor_result$p.value              # test against H₀: ρ = 0
cor_result$conf.int             # 95% CI for r

Pearson's r assumes both variables are continuous and approximately normally distributed, and that the relationship is linear (always plot first — Anscombe's quartet demonstrates that four datasets with identical r = 0.816 have completely different structures). Spearman's rho (ρ) is the non-parametric alternative, appropriate for ordinal data or non-normal distributions. It computes r on the ranks of the scores rather than their raw values:

cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")

A common misconception: a significant correlation does not mean the relationship is large. With n = 500, r = 0.09 reaches p < .05 but explains less than 1% of variance. Always report and interpret r (or r²), not just p.

Simple Linear Regression

Regression extends correlation by fitting a prediction equation: for a given value of the predictor (x), what score would we predict on the outcome (y)? The model is:

y = b₀ + b₁x + ε

where b₀ is the intercept (predicted y when x = 0), b₁ is the slope (change in y for each 1-unit increase in x), and ε is the residual error. R fits this using ordinary least squares (OLS): it finds the line that minimises the sum of squared differences between observed and predicted values.

model <- lm(stress ~ support, data = df)   # formula: outcome ~ predictor
summary(model)                              # full model output

The summary(model) output has three key sections:

Coefficients table:

            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  48.732      2.341   20.82  < 2e-16 ***
support      -0.417      0.034  -12.26  < 2e-16 ***
  • Estimate: b₀ (intercept) and b₁ (slope). Here: for every 1-point increase in social support, stress decreases by 0.417 points.
  • Pr(>|t|): p-value for H₀ that the coefficient equals zero. Three asterisks = p < .001.

R-squared (R²): The proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the predictor. In simple regression, R² = r². R² = 0.884 means 88.4% of the variance in stress scores is accounted for by social support.

F-statistic: Tests the overall model (H₀: all slopes = 0). In simple regression, F = t² for the slope. p < .05 means the model explains significantly more variance than the null (intercept-only) model.

Extracting Values from the Model

summary(model)$r.squared      # R²
summary(model)$coefficients   # full coefficient table as matrix
coef(model)                   # just the coefficients: intercept and slope
fitted(model)                 # predicted values (ŷ) for each observation
residuals(model)              # y - ŷ for each observation

Assumptions

Simple linear regression assumes: (1) linearity — the relationship between x and y is linear (check with a scatterplot); (2) independence of observations; (3) homoscedasticity — residuals have constant variance across predicted values; (4) normality of residuals. The function plot(model) produces four diagnostic plots: the residuals vs fitted plot (checks linearity and homoscedasticity) and the Q-Q plot (checks residual normality) are most important.

Correlation vs Regression: When to Use Which

Use correlation when you want to quantify the strength of association between two variables with no directional hypothesis. Use regression when you have a designated predictor and outcome variable, want to make predictions, or need to control for covariates (multiple regression). Both require the same assumption of a linear relationship and are vulnerable to the same problems: outliers inflate r and distort slopes, non-linearity makes linear models misleading, and neither establishes causation without a manipulative experimental design.

APA Reporting

Correlation: Social support was significantly negatively correlated with perceived stress, r(18) = −.94, p < .001, 95% CI [−.97, −.87].

Regression: Social support significantly predicted stress scores (b = −0.42, SE = 0.03), t(18) = −12.26, p < .001, R² = .89, F(1, 18) = 150.3, p < .001.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen loads a dataset from a student wellbeing survey: social support scores (MSPSS scale, 12–84) and perceived stress scores (PSS, 0–40) for 20 university students. She plots them first.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Always plot before you compute. The scatterplot shows a clear downward trend — more support, less stress. Now: how strong is that relationship? That's Pearson's r. cor.test(support, stress). Result: r = −0.94. Very strong. But that's the association — it doesn't tell me how much stress I'd predict for a given support score.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: For prediction, I need regression. lm(stress ~ support). The output gives me an equation. The slope is −0.42: for every extra point of social support, predicted stress drops by 0.42 points. The intercept — 48.7 — is the predicted stress when support is zero. Which in this context is clinically off the scale, but mathematically it's just where the line crosses the y-axis.
She pulls up summary(model). The R-squared is 0.884. A student asks what that means.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: R-squared is the proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the model. 0.884 means social support accounts for 88.4% of the variation in stress scores in this sample. That's high. In the real world, you'd be doing very well to explain 30–40% of variance in a complex outcome like stress. But this is also just one predictor — in reality you'd want to include sleep, financial situation, workload. That's multiple regression.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Critical point: this is a cross-sectional survey. The correlation and regression tell us the variables are strongly associated. They do not tell us that increasing someone's social support will reduce their stress. For causal inference you need experimental manipulation or, at minimum, longitudinal data with rigorous covariate control.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a clinician who has no statistics background what R-squared means in the context of predicting patient anxiety from a social support measure. What would R² = 0.20 mean, and what would R² = 0.80 mean? Why can't you conclude from a high R-squared that increasing social support will reduce anxiety?

rabbitHoleTerms.definition: The proportion of variance in the outcome variable explained by the predictor(s). In simple regression, R² = r². Values range from 0 (predictor explains nothing) to 1 (predictor explains all variation). R² = 0.40 means 40% of variability in the outcome is accounted for by the model.

R's lm() function fits regression models using OLS: it finds the slope and intercept that minimise the sum of squared vertical distances between observed data points and the fitted regression line (residuals). OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) under the Gauss-Markov assumptions.

The differences between observed values (y) and values predicted by the regression model (ŷ). Residuals should be randomly distributed around zero with constant variance (homoscedasticity) and approximate normality for OLS to be valid.

A non-parametric correlation coefficient computed on the ranks of the data rather than raw scores. Appropriate when variables are ordinal, distributions are non-normal, or there are outliers that would disproportionately influence Pearson's r.

Four datasets constructed by statistician Francis Anscombe (1973) with nearly identical means, variances, correlations (r ≈ 0.816), and regression lines — but radically different scatterplot shapes. A classic demonstration that summary statistics are insufficient without visual inspection of the data.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher finds r = −0.61, p = .002 between exam anxiety and exam performance. What percentage of variance in exam performance is explained by exam anxiety?
options: 61% (the r value directly)
78% (the square root of r)
0.2% (the p-value expressed as a percentage)
questions.explanationHtml: The coefficient of determination (r²) represents the proportion of variance in one variable explained by the linear relationship with the other. r² = (−0.61)² = 0.3721, meaning approximately 37.2% of variance in exam performance is associated with exam anxiety. The r value itself (0.61) is not a proportion of variance — it must be squared to yield r².

questions.questionHtml: In R, a researcher fits model <- lm(depression ~ sleep_quality) and finds the slope for sleep_quality is b = 1.43, p < .001. Sleep quality is measured by the PSQI (higher scores = worse sleep). What is the correct interpretation of b = 1.43?
options: For every 1-point increase in sleep quality (worse sleep), predicted depression score increases by 1.43 points
The correlation between sleep quality and depression is 1.43
R-squared for the model is 1.43, meaning the model explains 143% of variance
Participants with sleep problems scored 1.43 standard deviations higher on depression
questions.correctAnswer: For every 1-point increase in sleep quality (worse sleep), predicted depression score increases by 1.43 points
questions.explanationHtml: In linear regression, the slope coefficient (b) represents the predicted change in the outcome variable for each 1-unit increase in the predictor. Because higher PSQI scores mean worse sleep, b = 1.43 means that participants with 1 additional point of poor sleep quality are predicted to score 1.43 points higher on the depression measure. The positive slope indicates a positive relationship between sleep problems and depression.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: A significant Pearson correlation (r = −0.72, p < .001) between daily physical activity and depression scores in a cross-sectional survey establishes that increasing physical activity causes a reduction in depression.
questions.explanationHtml: Correlation does not establish causation. A cross-sectional survey observes variables at one time point without manipulation. The significant negative correlation could reflect: (1) activity reducing depression (the hypothesised causal direction); (2) depression reducing activity (reverse causation — depressed people exercise less); or (3) a third variable (e.g., overall health, sleep quality) causing both more activity and lower depression. Establishing causation requires experimental manipulation (random assignment to activity conditions) or, at minimum, longitudinal data with rigorous control for confounders.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher runs cor.test(neuroticism, wellbeing) and finds r = −0.12, p = .031 in a sample of n = 280. Another researcher runs the same test with n = 30 and finds r = −0.38, p = .038. Which result provides stronger evidence of a practically meaningful relationship?
options: The n = 280 result, because a larger sample provides more reliable estimates
The n = 30 result, because r = −0.38 is a larger effect size despite the similar p-values
Both results are equivalent because both achieve p < .05
Neither result, because neither p-value is below .001
questions.correctAnswer: The n = 30 result, because r = −0.38 is a larger effect size despite the similar p-values
questions.explanationHtml: Both results reach p < .05, but r = −0.12 (n = 280) is a trivially small effect (r² = 1.4% of variance explained) that only reaches significance because large samples have high power to detect even negligible effects. r = −0.38 (n = 30) is a small-to-medium effect (r² = 14.4% of variance explained) — substantially more meaningful even though the p-values are similar. This illustrates why effect sizes are more informative than p-values alone: the p-value conflates effect size and sample size, while r directly quantifies the relationship strength.

subChunks.title: One-Way ANOVA in R
subChunks.hookHtml: Suppose you're comparing three therapy conditions — CBT, mindfulness, and a waitlist control — on anxiety outcomes. You could run three separate t-tests (CBT vs. mindfulness, CBT vs. control, mindfulness vs. control). But conducting three t-tests inflates your Type I error rate: if each test has a 5% false positive risk, the probability of at least one false positive across three tests is nearly 15%. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) solves this by testing whether any group means differ in a single omnibus F-test, preserving the alpha level. When ANOVA is significant, post-hoc tests identify which specific groups differ — with the alpha controlled for multiple comparisons. This is the standard approach when comparing three or more groups on a continuous outcome, and it is omnipresent in clinical, experimental, and educational psychology research.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The F-Statistic: Signal-to-Noise

ANOVA partitions the total variability in the outcome into two sources:

  • Between-group variance (signal): how much the group means differ from the grand mean. Large between-group variance = the groups are genuinely different.
  • Within-group variance (noise): how much individual scores scatter around their own group mean. This is the natural variability that would exist even if groups were identical.

The F-statistic is the ratio of mean between-group variance (MS_between) to mean within-group variance (MS_within):

F = MS_between / MS_within

If the null hypothesis is true (all group means are equal), F ≈ 1 on average, because between-group differences reflect only sampling error — the same source as within-group noise. An F well above 1 suggests the between-group variation is too large to attribute to chance alone. The F-statistic is referred to an F-distribution with df₁ = k − 1 (where k = number of groups) and df₂ = N − k (where N = total sample size) to obtain the p-value.

One-Way ANOVA in R

# Requires a data frame with outcome and group columns
model <- aov(score ~ condition, data = therapy_data)
summary(model)

The summary() output for a one-way ANOVA:

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)
condition    2  341.6  170.8   89.94 1.2e-13 ***
Residuals   27   57.1    2.11
  • Df: degrees of freedom — k − 1 = 2 for condition (3 groups); N − k = 27 for residuals.
  • Sum Sq: SS_between (341.6) and SS_within (57.1). SS_total = 398.7.
  • Mean Sq: SS / Df — the variance estimates divided by their df.
  • F value: 170.8 / 2.11 = 80.9. Extremely large — the between-group signal greatly exceeds the noise.
  • Pr(>F): the p-value for H₀ that all three group means are equal.

Effect Size: Eta-Squared (η²)

Eta-squared (η²) is the ANOVA analogue of r²: the proportion of total variance in the outcome explained by the group factor.

η² = SS_between / SS_total

# Extract from summary output
ss <- summary(model)[[1]]$'Sum Sq'
eta_sq <- ss[1] / sum(ss)

By convention (Cohen, 1988): η² = .01 (small), .06 (medium), .14 (large). Partial eta-squared (η²ₚ) is reported in repeated-measures and factorial designs; in one-way ANOVA, η² and η²ₚ are identical. Omega-squared (ω²) is a less biased alternative to η², particularly in small samples: ω² = (SS_between − df_between × MS_within) / (SS_total + MS_within). R does not have a built-in ω² function but the effectsize package provides one.

Post-Hoc Tests: Tukey HSD

A significant omnibus F tells you that at least one group mean differs — it does not tell you which pairs differ. Post-hoc tests make all pairwise comparisons while controlling the family-wise error rate. Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) is the standard choice when group sizes are equal and homoscedasticity holds:

tukey <- TukeyHSD(model)
print(tukey)

Output example:

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
                          diff    lwr    upr  p adj
Mindfulness-CBT          3.2   2.01   4.39  0.0000
Control-CBT              8.2   7.01   9.39  0.0000
Control-Mindfulness      5.0   3.81   6.19  0.0000

diff = mean difference; lwr/upr = 95% simultaneous confidence intervals; p adj = p-value adjusted for multiple comparisons. All three pairs differ significantly here. The Bonferroni correction is a more conservative alternative (pairwise.t.test(score, condition, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni")) appropriate when group sizes are unequal or you have specific a priori hypotheses.

Assumptions

One-way ANOVA assumes: (1) normality of residuals within each group — check with shapiro.test(residuals(model)) or Q-Q plots; (2) homogeneity of variance (homoscedasticity) — check with Levene's test (car::leveneTest(score ~ condition, data = df)) or Bartlett's test (bartlett.test(score ~ condition, data = df)); (3) independence of observations. When homoscedasticity is violated, Welch's ANOVA is the appropriate alternative: oneway.test(score ~ condition, data = df, var.equal = FALSE), followed by Games-Howell post-hoc tests.

APA Reporting Format

A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of therapy condition on anxiety, F(2, 27) = 80.9, p < .001, η² = .86. Tukey post-hoc tests indicated that CBT (M = 8.3, SD = 1.49) produced significantly lower anxiety than both mindfulness (M = 11.5, SD = 1.43), p < .001, and waitlist control (M = 16.5, SD = 1.43), p < .001. Mindfulness also differed significantly from the control condition, p < .001.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen has a dataset from a randomised controlled trial: 30 participants randomly assigned to CBT (n = 10), mindfulness (n = 10), or a waitlist control (n = 10). Post-treatment GAD-7 scores are the outcome.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Three groups. You might think: run three t-tests. CBT vs. mindfulness, CBT vs. control, mindfulness vs. control. What is the problem with that?
A student answers: multiple comparisons inflate the Type I error rate. Dr. Chen nods.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Exactly. If each test has a 5% false positive rate, three tests give you nearly a 15% chance of at least one spurious significant result. ANOVA tests the omnibus question first — do any groups differ? — in a single test at alpha = .05. Then post-hoc tests identify which pairs differ, with the error rate controlled across all comparisons.
She types: model <- aov(score ~ condition, data = therapy_data). summary(model). F(2, 27) = 80.9, p < .001. Then: eta_sq <- ss[1] / sum(ss). 0.857.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Eta-squared of 0.86. The therapy condition explains 86% of the variance in post-treatment anxiety. For a clinical trial with tight randomisation and clean operationalisation, that is exceptional — and it should make you suspicious in the real world. An effect this large almost never replicates at scale. Here it is partly an artefact of very small within-group variance in our simulation.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: TukeyHSD(model). All three pairwise comparisons are significant. CBT outperforms mindfulness, mindfulness outperforms control, CBT substantially outperforms control. In a real paper you'd report the F statistic, df, p, and η², then report each Tukey comparison with mean differences and adjusted p-values. One ANOVA, one table. No inflation.

rabbitHoleTerms.definition: The test statistic for ANOVA: the ratio of mean between-group variance (MS_between) to mean within-group variance (MS_within). Under the null hypothesis (all means equal), F ≈ 1; substantially larger values indicate the group differences are unlikely to arise from chance alone.

An effect size measure for ANOVA: SS_between / SS_total. Represents the proportion of total outcome variance explained by the group factor. Cohen (1988) conventions: .01 small, .06 medium, .14 large. Mathematically equivalent to R² in the regression formulation of ANOVA.

Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference post-hoc test: makes all pairwise group comparisons while controlling the family-wise error rate at alpha = .05. Appropriate when group sizes are equal and homoscedasticity is met. More conservative than LSD but less conservative than Bonferroni.

The probability of committing at least one Type I error (false positive) across a family of related hypothesis tests. Running k comparisons each at alpha = .05 inflates the family-wise error rate toward 1 − (0.95)^k. ANOVA and post-hoc corrections control this rate.

An alternative to standard one-way ANOVA robust to violations of homoscedasticity (unequal group variances). In R: oneway.test(outcome ~ group, data = df, var.equal = FALSE). Followed by Games-Howell post-hoc tests rather than Tukey HSD.

A less biased alternative to eta-squared as an ANOVA effect size, particularly in small samples: ω² = (SS_between − df_between × MS_within) / (SS_total + MS_within). Corrects for the positive bias in η² when sample size is small relative to effect size.

questions.questionHtml: A one-way ANOVA comparing four groups (k = 4) with N = 60 total participants produces F(3, 56). What do the numbers in parentheses represent?
options: df_between = k − 1 = 3; df_within = N − k = 56
df_between = k = 4; df_within = N − 1 = 59
df_between = 3 groups compared; df_within = 56 pairwise comparisons
MS_between = 3; MS_within = 56
questions.explanationHtml: The F-statistic is reported as F(df_between, df_within). For a one-way ANOVA: df_between = k − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3 (degrees of freedom for the group factor); df_within = N − k = 60 − 4 = 56 (degrees of freedom for the residuals, also called the error term). These match the rows in the ANOVA summary table.

questions.questionHtml: A one-way ANOVA comparing three stress interventions yields F(2, 57) = 4.12, p = .021, η² = .13. Tukey HSD post-hoc tests show: intervention A vs. B: p = .019; A vs. C: p = .643; B vs. C: p = .082. What is the most accurate summary of these findings?
options: All three interventions differ significantly from each other
There is a significant overall effect; intervention A produces significantly lower stress than B, but neither differs significantly from C
There is no significant overall effect because not all pairwise comparisons are significant
The ANOVA is significant but Tukey post-hoc tests show the overall effect is a Type I error
questions.correctAnswer: There is a significant overall effect; intervention A produces significantly lower stress than B, but neither differs significantly from C
questions.explanationHtml: The omnibus F is significant (p = .021), confirming that at least one group mean differs. Tukey post-hoc tests identify which specific pairs differ while controlling family-wise error. Only A vs. B reaches the adjusted significance threshold (p = .019). A vs. C (p = .643) and B vs. C (p = .082) do not. The conclusion is that the overall effect is significant but driven primarily by the A-B difference; the pattern of pairwise results is not sufficient grounds to dismiss the omnibus finding as a false positive.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher compares cognitive scores across three educational levels (school, college, university). Levene's test returns p = .003, indicating significant heterogeneity of variance. Which is the most appropriate analysis?
options: Proceed with standard one-way ANOVA — ANOVA is robust to violations of homoscedasticity with equal group sizes
Use Welch's ANOVA (oneway.test with var.equal = FALSE) and Games-Howell post-hoc tests
Use a non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test, which has no variance assumption
Run three separate t-tests with Bonferroni correction instead of ANOVA
questions.correctAnswer: Use Welch's ANOVA (oneway.test with var.equal = FALSE) and Games-Howell post-hoc tests
questions.explanationHtml: When Levene's test indicates significant heteroscedasticity (p = .003), the homoscedasticity assumption is violated and standard one-way ANOVA may produce inflated Type I error rates. Welch's ANOVA (oneway.test with var.equal = FALSE) adjusts degrees of freedom to account for unequal variances — analogous to Welch's t-test. Games-Howell post-hoc tests (rather than Tukey HSD) are used in conjunction because they do not assume equal variances. The Kruskal-Wallis test is an alternative but sacrifices power and shifts to testing distributions rather than means.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: A significant one-way ANOVA result (p < .05) establishes that all group means differ significantly from each other.
questions.explanationHtml: A significant omnibus F-test only establishes that at least one group mean differs from at least one other — it specifies nothing about which pairs differ. It is possible that only two of three groups differ significantly from each other, with the third showing no significant difference from either. Post-hoc tests (Tukey HSD, Games-Howell, Bonferroni) are required to identify which specific pairwise comparisons reach significance while controlling the family-wise error rate.
